candidates.lesson_subject: Explicit web proxy isolation: PAC delivery, proxy-policy matching, and FortiIsolator handoff
candidates.feature_mechanism_fingerprint: Explicit proxy listener accepts browser-directed HTTP/HTTPS or PAC-selected traffic; proxy policy action isolate forwards selected sessions to a configured FortiIsolator server; PAC delivery is a separate transaction and stored per VDOM.
candidates.workflow_transaction_fingerprint: Browser retrieves PAC -> FindProxyForURL chooses PROXY or DIRECT -> client connects to explicit proxy listener -> proxy policy matches identity/destination -> accept or isolate action -> isolator receives selected request -> proxy and PAC transactions are logged separately.
candidates.failure_class: PAC content lost or unreachable after VDOM lifecycle operation; PAC 404; browser bypasses proxy; proxy policy matches but isolator server unreachable.
candidates.evidence_pattern: `get web-proxy explicit` proves PAC state; HTTPS GET/certificate chain proves PAC delivery; proxy-policy log action=isolate proves policy selection but not isolator health; traffic/session logs prove data path.
candidates.remediation_path: Validate VDOM PAC state, restore empty PAC data, use trusted certificate for HTTPS PAC, verify listener and proxy policy order, validate isolator address/port/reachability.
candidates.question_fingerprint: Browser fetches PAC but suspicious browsing is not isolated; distinguish PAC selection, proxy listener, policy action and isolator reachability.
candidates.diagram_topology_layout_fingerprint: Browser -> HTTPS PAC service -> explicit proxy listener -> proxy-policy decision -> normal egress or FortiIsolator; per-VDOM storage and certificate trust side notes.
candidates.scenario_age_note: Community VDOM/PAC issue is an older support scenario (about six months old), not a newly published 30-day case.

candidates.lesson_subject: FortiManager security boot chain: TPM, UEFI Secure Boot, self-encrypting drives and runtime file integrity
candidates.feature_mechanism_fingerprint: FortiManager platform security layers combine trusted-host GUI restriction, TPM-backed trust, UEFI Secure Boot, self-encrypting drive protection and runtime integrity verification of signed executables/libraries; boot-time BIOS checks precede filesystem load, runtime hash checks block unauthorized binaries/modules.
candidates.workflow_transaction_fingerprint: Power-on -> UEFI/BIOS validates signed boot components and TPM trust -> protected root filesystem starts -> executable hashes are loaded -> runtime write/module controls enforce integrity -> mismatch/missing hash generates security event and blocks execution/reboots.
candidates.failure_class: Boot integrity failure or runtime hash mismatch blocks binary execution and may reboot appliance; operator confuses encrypted storage with code integrity or treats a reboot as an ordinary service failure.
candidates.evidence_pattern: Boot/security event logs and file-integrity violation events prove integrity enforcement; TPM/secure-boot platform state proves boot trust; disk encryption protects data at rest but does not prove firmware integrity; trusted-host restrictions prove management-plane source restriction only.
candidates.remediation_path: Check appliance platform support and firmware version; review integrity event IDs and timestamps; preserve logs before reboot; validate signed firmware image and vendor-supported recovery/reflash; separately verify trusted-host and encryption configuration.
candidates.question_fingerprint: FortiManager reboots after a protected binary hash mismatch; distinguish boot-chain trust, runtime integrity enforcement and self-encrypting-drive confidentiality.
candidates.diagram_topology_layout_fingerprint: Power-on -> UEFI/TPM verification -> signed boot/root filesystem -> runtime executable hash gate -> normal process start or blocked binary/reboot; disk encryption shown as separate at-rest layer.
candidates.scenario_age_note: No recent directly matched FortiManager Community scenario surfaced in the product-area sweep.

candidates.lesson_subject: FortiAnalyzer 8.0 playbook execution: connector tasks, dry-run replay, node debugging and partial reruns
candidates.feature_mechanism_fingerprint: Playbook trigger plus linked connector tasks with JSON input/output dependencies; 8.0 adds step debugging, replay, partial restart, Branch/Wait/Compare/Switch controls and Jinja conditions/loops.
candidates.workflow_transaction_fingerprint: Trigger fires -> task receives trigger/previous-task JSON -> connector action runs -> output feeds downstream task -> branch/condition/loop controls execution -> job status and task errors persist; dry-run mock data is cleared on save/exit.
candidates.failure_class: Workflow task fails because connector inactive, JSON input schema wrong, downstream condition wrong or external API credentials/permissions unavailable.
candidates.evidence_pattern: Job ID/status and per-node input/output localize failure; inactive connectors are grayed; dry-run proves data mapping but not production credentials or external API health.
candidates.remediation_path: Activate connector, test credentials, replay with representative mock data, inspect each node input/output, run failing node alone, use partial rerun from corrected node.
candidates.question_fingerprint: Incident playbook fails at third task after upstream schema change; identify node-level output inspection and partial rerun.
candidates.diagram_topology_layout_fingerprint: Trigger -> Task 1 -> Branch/Compare -> Task 2 -> Wait -> Task 3; side loop for dry-run and partial restart.
candidates.scenario_age_note: Recent Community result concerned stale device status after reboot; it is included as a separate evidence-boundary case, not as the playbook's primary feature source.

candidates.lesson_subject: FortiSwitch storm control: traffic-class thresholds, burst handling, port overrides and drop telemetry
candidates.feature_mechanism_fingerprint: Storm control meters broadcast, unknown-unicast and unknown-multicast packet rates independently; global or port-level thresholds trigger drop or rate-limit behavior; burst-size levels tune short bursts; monitoring emits logs when dropped-packet rate crosses high-rate/filter threshold.
candidates.workflow_transaction_fingerprint: Enable selected traffic classes -> set pps threshold and burst level -> apply global or per-port override -> ASIC meters frames -> excess traffic is dropped/rate-limited -> monitor counter/log exposes sustained drop rate.
candidates.failure_class: Legitimate ARP/ND/multicast discovery or unknown-unicast convergence traffic is suppressed by overly low threshold; port override silently differs from global profile; rate=0 drops all enabled classes.
candidates.evidence_pattern: `get switch storm-control` and port config prove thresholds; `diagnose switch storm-control` proves drop rate/port; storm-control log proves threshold event but not application root cause; packet capture before/after switch localizes loss.
candidates.remediation_path: Baseline pps by traffic class, configure nonzero conservative threshold and burst, apply override only where needed, enable monitor/high-rate logs, compare ingress and egress captures before changing routing or spanning tree.
candidates.question_fingerprint: A new endpoint discovery storm causes intermittent ARP and service discovery failures on one access port; distinguish broadcast/unknown-multicast threshold drops from a loop.
candidates.diagram_topology_layout_fingerprint: Ingress port -> per-class packet-rate meters -> burst/threshold gate -> forwarded traffic or drop/rate-limit; telemetry branch to counters and log.
candidates.scenario_age_note: No recent directly matched FortiSwitch storm-control Community scenario surfaced.

candidates.lesson_subject: RADIUS VLAN name tags and round-robin VLAN pools on a single enterprise SSID
candidates.feature_mechanism_fingerprint: RADIUS Access-Accept Tunnel-Type=VLAN, Tunnel-Medium-Type=IEEE-802 and Tunnel-Private-Group-ID may return a VLAN ID, interface name or vlan-name key; a name key can map to up to eight VLAN IDs selected round-robin.
candidates.workflow_transaction_fingerprint: Client associates to one bridge SSID -> EAP/RADIUS -> Access-Accept returns name tag -> VAP vlan-name table resolves tag -> VLAN ID chosen -> client frames bridge into VLAN -> DHCP/policy apply.
candidates.failure_class: Authentication succeeds but client lands on default/wrong VLAN because Tunnel-Private-Group-ID does not match name-tag key, dynamic-vlan is off, or selected VLAN is missing from bridge path.
candidates.evidence_pattern: Access-Accept attributes prove returned tag; VAP show proves mapping; client table proves assigned VLAN; DHCP lease and trunk capture prove reachability; EAP success alone does not prove VLAN resolution.
candidates.remediation_path: Align exact RADIUS tag/key; enable dynamic-vlan; define one or multiple VLAN IDs (max eight); create VLAN interfaces/DHCP/policies and permit VLANs on trunks; verify round-robin assignment on new authentications.
candidates.question_fingerprint: One SSID authenticates all users but some clients receive default subnet; identify name-tag resolution and missing VLAN path.
candidates.diagram_topology_layout_fingerprint: Single SSID -> RADIUS Access-Accept name tag -> VAP mapping table -> round-robin VLAN pool -> DHCP/policy.

candidates.lesson_subject: FortiNAC high availability: primary/secondary control, MySQL replication and shared-IP failover
candidates.feature_mechanism_fingerprint: FortiNAC HA management process exchanges state between primary and secondary, controls which appliance is active, mirrors critical configuration and uses MySQL replication for database synchronization; optional shared IP moves to the active appliance.
candidates.workflow_transaction_fingerprint: HA-capable licenses and matching topology -> configure primary/secondary and gateway reachability -> primary establishes replication -> save/restart services -> management process monitors peer/database -> failover promotes secondary and moves shared IP/host name -> recovery resynchronizes state.
candidates.failure_class: Secondary does not take control because HA state is Idle, database replication is unhealthy, peer/gateway reachability is broken, or shared IP is configured across different subnets; secondary GUI may not be running until manually started for configuration.
candidates.evidence_pattern: HA state and replication status prove synchronization/role; gateway reachability proves one monitoring path only; shared-IP ownership proves management endpoint move but not application server pair health; secondary service state and agent communication prove service takeover.
candidates.remediation_path: Verify HA licensing and peer credentials, database replication and gateway monitor path; use shared IP only when both appliances are in same subnet; restart services after configuration; check Control Server/Application Server pairing and secondary GUI state.
candidates.question_fingerprint: Primary fails but secondary remains Idle despite network reachability; distinguish HA management process, MySQL replication and shared-IP constraints.
candidates.diagram_topology_layout_fingerprint: Primary/secondary HA pair with management process, MySQL replication, gateway monitors and movable shared IP; state transition Primary Active -> Secondary Active.

candidates.lesson_subject: TEAP chained machine-and-user authentication: outer tunnel, inner method ordering and policy result
candidates.feature_mechanism_fingerprint: EAP-TEAP establishes a protected outer TLS tunnel then performs configurable inner authentication methods; FortiNAC-F 7.6.3 supports primary computer authentication followed by secondary user authentication, or other supported combinations, enabling device and user identity in one 802.1X exchange.
candidates.workflow_transaction_fingerprint: Windows supplicant starts EAP-TEAP -> FortiNAC-F RADIUS virtual server negotiates outer TLS -> computer inner method authenticates machine -> user inner method authenticates interactive user -> FortiNAC policy evaluates both identities -> Access-Accept and port authorization.
candidates.failure_class: Outer TEAP TLS succeeds but second inner method fails because Windows supplicant mode/order differs from FortiNAC primary/secondary auth settings, or server/client trust and EAP method support are inconsistent.
candidates.evidence_pattern: RADIUS virtual server supported EAP list proves TEAP enabled; TEAP logs show outer tunnel and inner-method sequence; Windows EAP event log shows client method; Access-Accept proves final authorization but not both identities unless both inner stages are present.
candidates.remediation_path: Enable TLS and TEAP on virtual server; set primary Computer and secondary User when that order is intended; configure Windows Microsoft EAP-TEAP and User-or-Computer authentication; align trusted roots and verify both inner exchanges in RADIUS logs.
candidates.question_fingerprint: Outer TEAP TLS is successful but user login never reaches policy; identify mismatch in primary/secondary inner-auth ordering rather than changing VLAN policy.
candidates.diagram_topology_layout_fingerprint: Windows supplicant -> TEAP outer TLS -> inner computer authentication -> inner user authentication -> FortiNAC-F policy -> switch authorization.
candidates.semantic_distinction: The prior 11-21 lesson covered single-stage EAP-TTLS/PAP with Entra ID and Local RADIUS; this lesson covers TEAP's protected tunnel and sequential machine+user inner methods, not Entra TTLS/PAP.

candidates.lesson_subject: FortiAuthenticator RADIUS proxy transparency and Message-Authenticator enforcement
candidates.feature_mechanism_fingerprint: Remote RADIUS profile can proxy original authentication method unchanged; optional realm preservation retains qualified username; FAC sends Message-Authenticator as RADIUS client and can require it in upstream responses.
candidates.workflow_transaction_fingerprint: NAS -> FAC RADIUS proxy -> primary/secondary upstream RADIUS -> FAC validates response Message-Authenticator if required -> NAS receives Access-Accept/Reject.
candidates.failure_class: Proxy authentication fails due to unsupported upstream auth method, realm rewrite, missing Message-Authenticator or upstream timeout.
candidates.evidence_pattern: Remote profile settings prove Proxy mode/realm/timeout; packet capture proves attributes and Message-Authenticator; FAC debug identifies upstream reject/timeout; Access-Accept alone does not prove accounting or integrity policy.
candidates.remediation_path: Use Proxy when upstream supports original auth method; preserve realm when required; enable response Message-Authenticator enforcement only after upstream compatibility check; configure timeout/secondary server and inspect both RADIUS legs.
candidates.question_fingerprint: FAC relays Access-Requests but upstream accepts only some clients after hardening; distinguish method transparency, realm preservation and response integrity validation.
candidates.diagram_topology_layout_fingerprint: NAS -> FAC RADIUS proxy -> primary/secondary RADIUS with request passthrough and response Message-Authenticator validation.

candidates.lesson_subject: FortiPAM Web RDP connection-broker load-balancing cookie propagation
candidates.feature_mechanism_fingerprint: FortiPAM 1.9 Web RDP target exposes Loading Balancing Information to pass a connection-broker load-balancing cookie; target must use a template with Web RDP default launcher; CLI value must preserve `tsv://MS Terminal Services` prefix.
candidates.workflow_transaction_fingerprint: Create/edit Web RDP target -> choose compatible secret template/default launcher -> configure load-balancing info cookie -> launch Web RDP secret -> FortiPAM passes cookie to Microsoft Terminal Services connection broker -> broker selects correct farm/collection host -> browser session attaches.
candidates.failure_class: Web RDP launch reaches broker but lands on wrong host or fails farm selection because cookie is missing/malformed, template does not use Web RDP default launcher, or required prefix is absent.
candidates.evidence_pattern: Target configuration and template prove attribute is set and supported; launch logs/connection-broker logs prove cookie receipt and host selection; successful FortiPAM authentication alone does not prove broker affinity.
candidates.remediation_path: Use Web RDP default launcher template; set `rdp-load-balancing-info` with required `tsv://MS Terminal Services` prefix and exact farm token; verify broker logs and target selection; do not apply to native RDP or unrelated launcher templates.
candidates.question_fingerprint: Web RDP authentication succeeds but broker selects an unbalanced farm node; identify the target-level load-balancing cookie and template constraint.
candidates.diagram_topology_layout_fingerprint: FortiPAM Web RDP launcher -> target-specific load-balancing cookie -> Microsoft Connection Broker -> selected RDS farm host -> browser session.

candidates.lesson_subject: FortiSIEM Windows Agent File Integrity Monitoring hashes: SHA-256 evidence and threat-intelligence correlation
candidates.feature_mechanism_fingerprint: FortiSIEM Windows Agent FIM monitors configured file/folder paths and reports file integrity changes; agent release 3.1.0 changed FIM file hashes from MD5 to SHA-256 to align with external threat-intelligence hash feeds.
candidates.workflow_transaction_fingerprint: Windows Agent monitor template defines watched paths/operations -> agent observes file create/modify/delete -> computes SHA-256 for file/folder evidence -> event is sent to Collector/Supervisor -> FortiSIEM parser normalizes hash/path/host -> analyst compares hash to threat intelligence and investigates.
candidates.failure_class: FIM alert absent because path/store is not in monitor template or agent lacks access; hash lookup misses because an external feed expects SHA-256 but stale MD5 value or path normalization is used.
candidates.evidence_pattern: Agent template proves path and operation coverage; agent event/log proves observation; parsed event proves host/path/hash reached FortiSIEM; SHA-256 equality proves content identity, not maliciousness by itself; absence of an event does not prove file was unchanged if monitoring scope is incomplete.
candidates.remediation_path: Validate agent version and monitor template, permissions and path scope; test a controlled file modification; verify SHA-256 in agent and parsed event; compare with trusted threat-intel feed and investigate signer/path/parent process before containment.
candidates.question_fingerprint: A Windows FIM event is present but threat-feed hash match fails after agent upgrade; identify SHA-256 versus legacy MD5 and scope/normalization boundaries.
candidates.diagram_topology_layout_fingerprint: Windows file system -> FIM monitor template -> agent SHA-256 event -> FortiSIEM Collector/Parser -> threat-intel comparison -> investigation.

candidates.lesson_subject: FortiSASE IPsec remote-agent application-based split tunneling: route scope and platform boundaries
candidates.feature_mechanism_fingerprint: FortiSASE IPsec remote-agent profiles support split tunneling; Windows FortiClient supports application-based split tunnel or full tunnel, while other platforms support full tunnel only. Split tunneling is a route/application inclusion decision and is separate from split DNS, agent policy and security-profile inspection.
candidates.workflow_transaction_fingerprint: FortiClient establishes IPsec agent tunnel -> endpoint profile and tunnel mode are applied -> Windows application-based split-tunnel rules classify app flows -> selected traffic enters IPsec to Security PoP, other traffic uses local route -> FortiSASE security policy handles tunneled flows.
candidates.failure_class: Some applications bypass expected SASE inspection because app-based split-tunnel match is wrong or unsupported OS is assumed to support split tunnel; existing SSL-to-IPsec transition is misconfigured and causes session disruption.
candidates.evidence_pattern: Endpoint profile proves IPsec tunnel type and split-tunnel policy; FortiClient route/app diagnostics prove local-vs-tunnel decision; PoP logs prove tunneled flow; absence from PoP logs alone does not prove block if app was intentionally excluded; successful IKE proves tunnel but not app selection.
candidates.remediation_path: Confirm instance supports IPsec remote agents and recommended FortiClient version; Windows-only application split-tunnel support; configure endpoint profile rules and test target application; use software audit best-practice for SSL-to-IPsec transition; plan maintenance because sessions may briefly disrupt.
candidates.question_fingerprint: Windows user sees a business app bypass the SASE PoP while another app is inspected; distinguish application-based split tunnel from split DNS and IPsec tunnel establishment.
candidates.diagram_topology_layout_fingerprint: Windows FortiClient app flow classifier -> tunneled application traffic to FortiSASE PoP; excluded app traffic follows local interface; IPsec control plane shown separately.
candidates.semantic_distinction: The prior 11-17 lesson covered split DNS domain-resolution steering; this lesson covers application/route forwarding decisions for IPsec remote agents, not DNS response selection.

candidates.lesson_subject: SD-WAN zones as route interfaces: multi-zone IPv4/IPv6 static routes and service-rule preference
candidates.feature_mechanism_fingerprint: SD-WAN members are grouped into logical zones; policies use zones rather than individual members; FortiOS 8.0 allows IPv4/IPv6 static routes to reference one or more zones and service rules to express zone preference, decoupling route intent from physical member identity.
candidates.workflow_transaction_fingerprint: Create SD-WAN zones -> assign members -> add IPv4/IPv6 static route with `sdwan-zone` list -> add service rule with `priority-zone` -> route lookup selects zone -> SD-WAN rule chooses eligible member within preferred zone based on strategy/health.
candidates.failure_class: Route or service rule references wrong zone or old `sdwan` syntax; route exists but zone has no eligible members; operator expects member interface to be usable directly in policy after zone assignment.
candidates.evidence_pattern: `get router info routing-table` proves route installation/selected zone; `diagnose sys sdwan` proves member/zone state; service-rule counters/debug prove rule selection; a route to zone does not prove any member is healthy or traffic is permitted by firewall policy.
candidates.remediation_path: Verify zone membership and member health; configure static route using `set sdwan-zone` for IPv4/IPv6; use `set priority-zone` for service rule preference; verify firewall policies reference zone; migrate legacy `sdwan`/`virtual-wan-link` syntax as appropriate.
candidates.question_fingerprint: An IPv6 static route points at an SD-WAN member that was moved into a named zone; identify the zone-based route interface and distinguish route resolution from member health.
candidates.diagram_topology_layout_fingerprint: IPv4/IPv6 route lookup -> SD-WAN zone A/B -> member health/strategy selection -> WAN/overlay interface; parallel service rule zone preference.
